title: Suicide and Violence Risk Assessment Guide
sources: Resnick P. Suicide and Violence Risk Assessment. UH Psychiatry Didactics
Resnick P. Suicide Risk Assessment Update. UH Psychiatry Grand Rounds
Magellan Healthcare Practice Guideline for Assessing and Managing the Suicidal Patient
APA Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors
APA Resource Document on Psychiatric Violence Risk Assessment
disclaimer: Guidelines only — not a standard of medical care. Ultimate judgment is the treating provider's based on individual clinical data.
checklist: Identify acute vs chronic risk factors; static vs dynamic
Document treatment plan for acute/dynamic risk factors
documentation_template: A risk assessment was performed during this visit. Acute risk of suicide and self-harm is [low/moderate/high] [due to/despite] [factors]. Chronic risk of suicide is [low/moderate/high] [due to/despite] [factors]. Acute risk of violence is [low/moderate/high] [due to/despite] [factors]. Chronic risk of violence is [low/moderate/high] [due to/despite] [factors]. Ongoing risk will be mitigated by [risk reduction strategies].

suicide_risk_levels.high: Severe psychiatric symptoms or acute precipitating event; protective factors not relevant; potentially lethal attempt or persistent ideation with strong intent/rehearsal
suicide_risk_levels.moderate: Multiple risk factors, few protective factors; ideation with plan but not intent or behavior
suicide_risk_levels.low: Modifiable risk factors, strong protective factors; thoughts of death without plan, intent, or behavior

violence_risk_levels_note: Use same low/moderate/high framing; assess acute vs chronic separately
suicide_warning_signs: Threatening or planning self-harm; seeking lethal means
Talking/writing about death or suicide (including social media)
Affairs in order, giving possessions away, unexpected visits
Sudden improvement after decision to die by suicide
suicide_acute_dynamic_factors: Current/prior suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, behavior (plan > thoughts; lethality matters)
Severe anxiety, akathisia, panic, insomnia, agitation, impulsivity, hopelessness, anhedonia
Command hallucinations, mood-congruent delusions, psychological turmoil
Life crisis, shame, humiliation, recent loss; exposure to suicide
Treatment access gaps, nonadherence, abrupt lithium discontinuation
suicide_chronic_static_factors: Prior attempts, family suicide history, trauma/abuse, borderline/antisocial traits
Demographics: male, older adult, youth, veteran, rural, sexual minority, unmarried
Chronic psychiatric illness severity and comorbidity
suicide_chronic_dynamic_factors: Post-discharge or treatment transition; chronic pain or fatal medical illness
Substance abuse; access to lethal means; social isolation; unemployment; bullying
violence_acute_dynamic_factors: Command hallucinations, persecutory delusions, lack of insight
violence_chronic_factors: Prior violence history, antisocial/borderline traits, nonadherence
Male, young age, weapons access, substance abuse, social isolation
Military/weapons training, low SES, family turmoil
protective_factors: Religious/spiritual beliefs, moral objections to suicide, fear of act or disapproval
Positive social support, employment, coping skills, hopefulness, reality testing
risk_reduction_strategies: Lethal means reduction; collateral; medication adjustment
Outpatient follow-up and communication with treater
Family/friend support; coping skills; 24/7 or medication supervision
Safety plan; crisis resources (988); consider lithium, clozapine, ketamine, ECT for severe cases

appendix_highlights.ed_discharge_after_attempt: May be possible when suicidality is reactive to precipitant with changed view, low-lethality plan/intent, stable/supportive housing, cooperative follow-up
appendix_highlights.chronic_elevated_risk: Focus dynamic factors, protective factors, stressors, lethal means vs baseline; document why inpatient care not indicated when applicable
appendix_highlights.contingency_statements: Contingent suicide threats may express unmet needs vs imminent risk — interpret in context

population_specific.veterans: PTSD, TBI, assault in service, transition times, clinical depression, comorbidity
population_specific.schizophrenia: Realistic illness awareness, higher education/aspirations, chronic deterioration
population_specific.bipolar: Highest suicide risk in depression > mixed > mania
population_specific.youth_10_24: Stressful events, disorders, substance, family conflict, bullying, self-harm, peer suicide exposure
population_specific.post_discharge_90_days: Recent self-harm, severe mental illness, first psychotic episode

mak_usage: Help residents identify and reflect on factors they considered — not to stratify risk
NEVER assign or state low/moderate/high (or any) suicide or violence risk level for a patient
NEVER say a patient is high risk, moderate risk, or low risk — that is the treating provider's judgment only
NEVER fill in, suggest, or complete documentation template language with risk levels
Suggest lattice placement for safety-planning learning captures only
If resident asks Mak to rate risk: redirect to their attending, safety plan, and factors they documented
Do not recite factor lists unprompted
mak_prohibitions: Stating patient is at imminent risk
Replacing clinical supervision or emergency services (988, ED)
